overview:
A regional quarrel in the Balkans became a world war in about five weeks. When a Bosnian Serb nationalist shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, Austria-Hungary saw a chance to settle accounts with Serbia; Germany backed it, Russia mobilised for Serbia, France was bound to Russia, and Britain entered when German armies drove through neutral Belgium. Historians still argue over how much of the July Crisis was miscalculation and how much was deliberate risk-taking in Berlin and Vienna, and the question has never fully settled. What is clear is that the war the generals expected did not arrive. The German sweep into France was halted on the Marne in September 1914, and the Western Front congealed into a line of trenches from the Channel to Switzerland that barely moved for three years. In the east there was more movement but no less killing: German victory at Tannenberg in August 1914, Russian success against Austria-Hungary in Galicia, and an Ottoman winter catastrophe at Sarikamish. Industrial societies proved able to feed men and shells into this system almost indefinitely. Verdun and the Somme in 1916 together cost roughly two million casualties and moved the front by a few miles.

The war was never only European. The Ottoman Empire's entry pulled in Gallipoli, Mesopotamia, Palestine and the Caucasus; German colonies in Africa and the Pacific were seized within months, though a German force in East Africa was still fighting on Armistice Day; Japan took German holdings in China and the Pacific; and the naval war ran to the South Atlantic, where a British squadron destroyed von Spee's ships off the Falklands in December 1914. More than six million of the roughly sixty-five million men mobilised came from outside Europe. Around a million Indian soldiers served overseas, and France recruited close to half a million men from West and North Africa, Madagascar and Indochina, much of it under pressure that colonial officials themselves could not honestly call voluntary. At sea, the one great fleet action at Jutland in 1916 was tactically ambiguous but left the British blockade intact, and it was the German answer to that blockade — unrestricted submarine warfare — that helped bring the United States in during April 1917.

Nineteen-seventeen broke the war open. Revolution removed Russia from the fighting, confirmed by the punitive Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918; the Italian front collapsed at Caporetto; Britain bled itself in the mud of Passchendaele. Germany used its freedom in the east for the Spring Offensive of 1918, which tore holes in the Allied line and then ran out of men, while American troops arrived at a rate Germany could not match. The Central Powers came apart from the periphery inward — Bulgaria, then the Ottomans, then Austria-Hungary — and Germany, facing mutiny and revolution at home, signed an armistice on 11 November 1918. Somewhere around ten million soldiers and several million civilians were dead, the latter figure especially uncertain because it mixes battlefield deaths with famine under blockade, the Armenian genocide, and the influenza pandemic the war helped spread. The Paris Peace Conference of 1919 then redrew much of the map, dissolving four empires and leaving grievances that outlived everyone who signed.
significance: The war ended the long nineteenth century and the European order that had run the world. Four dynastic empires — Romanov, Hohenzollern, Habsburg, Ottoman — vanished, replaced by nation-states, mandates and a Bolshevik government whose existence shaped the rest of the century. It normalised total mobilisation of civilian economies, mass propaganda, aerial bombing and chemical weapons, and it broke the assumption that European powers could fight limited wars among themselves. The peace settlement created both the League of Nations and the resentments that Nazi Germany later exploited, while in India, Egypt, Vietnam and much of Africa the gap between wartime sacrifice and postwar treatment fed nationalist movements that would dismantle the empires within two generations. Almost every large political question of the twentieth century — communism, fascism, decolonisation, the redrawn Middle East — runs back through 1914 to 1918.
coverage: Written from the reference works cited plus the 1914-1918-Online scholarly encyclopedia, whose own entries stress how unreliable casualty statistics are: armies concealed losses, the "missing" category mixed the dead with prisoners, and civilian death estimates range from about 1.5 to 4.2 million depending on method. The 186 events here skew heavily toward named battles and the European and Near Eastern fronts; home fronts, the blockade, the Armenian genocide, the African and Asian campaigns, women's war work, and the 1918 influenza pandemic are thinly represented or absent, and the surviving record for colonial and Ottoman soldiers is far poorer than for British, French and German ones.
